newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain and Portugal demand a hearing on euro claims.
newsitem.headline: Spain and Portugal demand a hearing on euro claims.

text.p: Spain and Portugal, eager to calm shaky domestic markets, have raised angry voices to try to penetrate the din of debate around Europe's monetary union and ensure their partners don't turn a deaf ear to their dramatic economic progress.

Spanish central bank governor Luis Angel Rojo and Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato took advantage of a Latin American forum in Barcelona this week to press Spain's claim to join Europe's common currency from the start in 1999 and to rail against anyone who said otherwise.
"There is no doubt we will be able to fulfil the criteria," Rato told Reuters Financial Televison on the fringes of the annual meeting of the Inter-American Development Bank.
"Some people in Europe should not be speaking about other countries. They should be concentrating on (their own house). That is what we are doing," Rato said.

Portuguese Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco lashed out at the term "Club Med," shorthand for the EU's Mediterranan states and the assumption that if Italy fails to qualify for the 1999 launch of the euro, Spain and Portugal must also be excluded.
"I do not think the decision about the single currency is going to be taken on geographical terms," he said in Brussels.

The new strident tone has been triggered by market tumult at home in the face of confusing and contradictory comments from Germany. Although one of the cornerstone of economic and monetary union (EMU), Bonn is struggling itself to meet the economic conditions for membership.

A continuing debate on whether the project should be delayed was sparked by German Finance Secretary Juergen Stark, who said in late January that some countries did not have the economic track record to join in the euro launch.
Although he named no names, market participants believed he was targeting Italy, Spain and Portugal.
The resulting single currency uncertainty has shaken Spanish and Portuguese markets and undone some of the gains driven by progress in fulfilling the EMU criteria.

The spread between Spanish and Portuguese bonds and German bunds -- a measure of the added risk of holding their debt -- rebounded from historic lows at the end of January of 83 and 80 basis points, respectively, to current levels of 134 and 118 as uncertainty rose. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point.

The Spanish spread dropped dramatically from 330 basis points a year ago as the peseta stabilised, inflation dived and the government put forward a strict 1997 budget -- making the nation's European aspirations possible.
"Now we are in the worst possible situation, with high spreads," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid. "Spain is putting as much pressure on as it can."
The Maastricht Treaty lays down economic targets on inflation, interest and exchange rates, budget deficits and public debt which nations must meet this year to join the euro from the start.

The treaty calls for debt to total no more than 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- or at least show significant progress in falling toward this level -- and for deficits to be three percent or less of GDP, except in exceptional circumstances.
Germany's economic convergence plan calls for a debt ratio of 61.5 percent of GDP this year. As the level is also rising, this does not meet the definition laid down in the treaty.

Spain and Portugal both have excessive but declining debt ratios. Spain's debt burden is seen falling to 67 percent this year from 69 percent in 1996, while Portugal's should fall to a revised 64.3 percent from 65.4
The Spanish deficit to gross domestic product should fall to three percent from 4.4 percent, while Portugal's is expected to decline to 2.9 percent from four.
Bank of Spain governor Rojo was not accommodating over Germany's plight.
"Germany has important economic and political problems in relation to the monetary union as other countries do and it is not totally clear how things will end," he said.

But Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres magnanimously suggested from Lisbon on Tuesday that Germany could join in the launch of the euro even if it failed to pass all the entry tests, given that the reasons for the miss were temporary and not structural.
He said a single currency without Germany would make little sense.
Darren Williams, senior economist at UBS in London, said it was up to Spain and Portugal to keep the pressure high to guarantee their voices were heard.

"It's up to them to keep things going," Williams said. "They think they're being unfairly treated. Five years ago they were told if they did XY and Z, they would join. Now they are being told something else."
